brief.head: No cricket next time
brief.text: Reboot civil­i­sa­tion from human na­ture alone, Amit Varma said, and money and foot­ball would prob­a­bly re­turn. Cricket would not: “It’s a his­tor­i­cal ac­ci­dent.” {063-C04}[[x3]]

brief.head: Prison mathematics
brief.text: Thrown into soli­tary con­fine­ment with only pen and paper, Ajay Shah would re­build all the math­e­mat­ics he knows. “Now re­build the whole damn ed­i­fice from scratch,” he said. {063-S03}

brief.head: Chess needs company
brief.text: Stefan Zweig’s pris­oner mas­tered chess[[x4]] against him­self. Amit Varma ar­gued a human brain hits a ceil­ing that way: every game with an op­po­nent is a con­ver­sa­tion[[x5]]. {063-C11}

brief.head: Beat the sugar pill
brief.text: In one wartime story, a pa­tient told he had been given anaes­thetic felt noth­ing dur­ing surgery. So a medicine must beat a placebo, Amit Varma said, not merely noth­ing. {063-C10}

brief.head: Why quackery caught on
brief.text: Homeopathy spread in the 19th cen­tury, Amit Varma said, when blood­let­ting was the cure for most things. Sugar pills at least would not kill you. {063-S10}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on what humanity forgets
lead.head: What the ocean of time took

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 63

body: Ajay Shah opened with a warn­ing. We think of knowl­edge as wealth that only grows, he said, but “in this episode today, we’re going to scare the be­je­sus out of you on this.”

Amit Varma began with a witch. In a thought ex­per­i­ment by the writer Tim Urban[[x1]], a wicked witch makes every ma­te­rial good on Earth van­ish. That leaves 7.3 bil­lion naked peo­ple with all their knowl­edge in their heads, and a note: build one work­ing iPhone 6S and ev­ery­thing comes back. {063-S01}
How long would that take? “Never,” said Shah. “It’s im­pos­si­ble.”

Without mar­kets, laws and in­sti­tu­tions, he said, “there is no way to feed seven and a half bil­lion peo­ple.” Humanity would sink into bar­barism, and the pop­u­la­tion would crash to 10 mil­lion. A new civil­i­sa­tion would rise, but never by the same path to touch screens.
## Sediment and the sea

Varma framed the theme with a line from a poem by Philip Larkin, in which mis­ery “deep­ens like a coastal shelf”. We like to think knowl­edge builds that way, each gen­er­a­tion lay­ing down a layer and stand­ing on the shoul­ders of gi­ants.
“So maybe it’s a good metaphor,” he said, “be­cause a lot of the sed­i­men­tary lay­ers get washed away by the ocean of time.” {063-C01}
Some lost knowl­edge has been re­gained, some is still being chased and some may never come back. The hosts told five such quests.
## Five quests
Silphium, a herb the Romans called the food of the gods, van­ished within a cou­ple of hun­dred years. A Turkish sci­en­tist may have found it again in Greece and Turkey.
Dhaka muslin, woven by six­teen vil­lages from a plant on the banks of the Meghna, had around 1,200 threads to the square inch. A re­vival has reached 300.
Fogbank, an aero­gel in­side an American atomic bomb, could not be re­made from its own ar­chives, not even by the re­tired sci­en­tists who wrote them.

Artemisinin, now the main­stay of malaria treat­ment, came from Tu Youyou’s care­ful read­ing of an an­cient Chinese text. And West Germany and Japan re­built after the Second World War with the knowl­edge their peo­ple still car­ried.
## What sur­vives

Shah’s ad­vice was to watch for records. Recovery de­pends on “the pres­ence of writ­ten records, the pres­ence of sam­ples, the pres­ence of fin­ished Dhaka muslin that you could then as­pire to re­verse en­gi­neer”. {063-C06}
Records alone are not enough. “If you don’t do some­thing for 30, 40 years, then there is a whole range of tacit knowl­edge that gets lost,” Shah said. {063-C05}
On an­cient texts he was blunt. “Two state­ments are true,” he said. “One, that most of that knowl­edge is rub­bish. Two, that some of it is mind blow­ingly great.”
Varma drew a rule for tra­di­tion: “we should be deeply scep­ti­cal of it, but never dis­mis­sive.” {063-C09} A rem­edy earns be­lief, he said, only once it passes the sci­en­tific method.
He also left a rid­dle. Survivors of the apoc­a­lypse find an iPhone 6S thou­sands of years later, plug it in and read its SMS mes­sages. What will they call them? “Ancient texts.”

second.label: Traditional medicine
second.head: Cold water, hot result
second.deck: Ajay Shah on Tu Youyou, who read an ancient text more carefully

pic.caption: Tu Youyou in 2015
pic.credit: Bengt Nyman from Vaxholm, Sweden, CC BY 2.0

body: In 1974, dur­ing the Vietnam War, Tu Youyou was sent to help Vietnam, Ajay Shah said, and its peo­ple asked for help with one thing: malaria. {#deputed} The par­a­site was grow­ing re­sis­tant to qui­nine.

About two thou­sand plants from an­cient Chinese texts had al­ready been tested and failed, and pa­pers said worm­wood did not work. Tu was not a PhD, but she was a mas­ter of clas­si­cal Chinese. She read one pas­sage as call­ing for cold ex­trac­tion: the plant soaked in water, un­heated.

She tried it on twenty pa­tients, and all twenty re­cov­ered. {#twenty} Later sci­en­tists found the part of the mol­e­cule that at­tacks the par­a­site and built stronger de­riv­a­tives. Artemisinin is now the world’s main­stay against malaria. {063-S08}

quote.text: You should re­mem­ber a woman look­ing at the mis­ery of malaria in Vietnam and doing re­search with the worm­wood tree in China

third.head: Guard duty, reason unknown

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the guard and the bench

body: An army camp keeps a guard be­side a gar­den bench[[x2]] 24 hours a day, chang­ing shifts every eight hours. The bench has no strate­gic or tac­ti­cal sig­nif­i­cance. Amit Varma told the story after the Fogbank tale.
A new com­man­dant asks why. The guard has been told to stand there. The deputy has no idea. Previous com­man­dants say it has al­ways been like this.
Obsessed, the com­man­dant tracks down the camp’s founder, now 93 and bedrid­den on a farm, flies out in econ­omy and talks his way past the wor­ried wife. {#ninetythree}
Why, he asks, does a guard stand be­side the bench? The old man looks at him with wiz­ened eyes. “What are you say­ing? The paint hasn’t dried yet.” {063-S07}

p2.title: Lost and found
p2.deck: Five quests for vanished knowledge, and the lessons Amit Varma and Ajay Shah drew from them

from1.head: What the ocean of time took

quote.text: There is no way to feed seven and a half bil­lion peo­ple with­out the glo­ries of the mar­ket econ­omy and mod­ern civil­i­sa­tion

box.title: The witch behind the episode
box.text: Tim Urban’s iPhone thought ex­per­i­ment reached Amit Varma when a friend shared it in a four-man WhatsApp group called Food Lovers of Mumbai. It shows how much of what we know de­pends on a web no one could quickly re­build. {063-R01}

sections.label: The premise
sections.head: Naked, clever and helpless
sections.caption: the wicked witch’s challenge
body: Amit Varma brought the ques­tion from a WhatsApp group: a post by the writer Tim Urban about a wicked witch who makes every ma­te­rial good on Earth van­ish, and prom­ises it all back once hu­man­ity builds one work­ing iPhone 6S. {063-R01}

Urban, Varma said, built up to it on Lex Fridman’s pod­cast by not­ing that no human being knows how to make a pen­cil. Leonard Read’s essay *I, Pencil*[[x7]][[x6]] tells the story from the pencil’s side: so many coun­tries, ma­te­ri­als and kinds of knowl­edge go into it that no one per­son can make one. {063-R03}

“Self-sufficiency is a myth,” Varma said. What we have in­stead is a “mag­nif­i­cent com­pli­cated in­ter­linked web of knowl­edge and peo­ple and spe­cial­i­sa­tion”. {063-C02} Frédéric Bastiat, he noted, wrote about how Paris gets fed with no one plan­ning it.
## Prices as tech­nol­ogy

Rebuilding would need more than ma­chines, Varma ar­gued. It would need what he called so­cial tech­nol­ogy: prices, for in­stance, which carry in­for­ma­tion and in­cen­tives be­tween peo­ple who never meet, as Friedrich Hayek ex­plained in *The Use of Knowledge in Society*. {063-C03}

Ajay Shah thought the witch’s chal­lenge could never be met. Without mar­kets and in­sti­tu­tions, peo­ple would turn on each other, as in Cormac McCarthy’s *The Road*, and the world pop­u­la­tion would crash to 10 mil­lion. {#tenmillion}
~ A new sci­en­tific civil­i­sa­tion would arise, Shah said, but it would not re­trace the pre­cise jour­ney to semi­con­duc­tors, in­te­grated cir­cuits and touch screens.

quote.text: There is no way to feed seven and a half bil­lion peo­ple with­out the glo­ries of the mar­ket econ­omy and mod­ern civil­i­sa­tion

art.caption: Amit Varma on the wicked witch’s challenge

sections.label: Quest one
sections.head: Food of the gods, gone
sections.caption: the lost Roman herb
body: The Romans wrote and wrote and wrote, Ajay Shah said, recipes in­cluded. Their texts prize a herb called sil­phium, which grew in what they called Carthage and we call Libya. Nobody could cul­ti­vate it, so for­agers gath­ered it from the wild, and it fetched the high­est prices.
Within a cou­ple of hun­dred years it was gone; leg­end has it that the last plant went to the Emperor Nero. {063-S04} Amit Varma added that Pliny the Elder recorded this in his *Natural History*.
## A mod­ern sec­ond chance

Expeditions into Libya’s re­motest moun­tains found noth­ing. Then a Turkish sci­en­tist found a plant of the Ferula fam­ily in re­mote parts of Greece and Turkey that looks a lot like the an­cient draw­ings. Food con­nois­seurs fed the old recipes call the re­sults mind-blowing.

Without an­cient bi­o­log­i­cal ma­te­rial there can be no DNA test, Shah said. But mod­ern sci­ence has done what the Romans could not: “they have ap­plied tools of mod­ern sci­ence to fig­ure out how to cul­ti­vate this in a green­house.” {#greenhouse}
~ The find is being kept quiet for now, Shah said, lest a stam­pede of for­agers, and spec­i­mens on eBay, drive the plant ex­tinct a sec­ond time. {#ebay}

quote.text: It would be lovely to not lose our knowl­edge.

sections.label: Quest two
sections.head: Many hands, no notebook
sections.caption: how a cloth was forgotten
body: Amit Varma, a Bengali, took up a Bengali loss. Dhaka muslin came from a plant on the banks of the Meghna and took six­teen vil­lages to make, each doing one part of the work. {#sixteen}

Each vil­lage knew its own stage, and no­body wrote the process down. When the trade died, the knowl­edge was lost within a gen­er­a­tion. {063-S05} “There is no Pliny the Elder to write down all the pro­cesses,” Varma said.
## Clues in a mu­seum

Recovery, Ajay Shah said, de­pends on what sur­vives. Here it was plant sam­ples in a London herbar­ium, which could be se­quenced, and fin­ished cloth in the Victoria and Albert Museum. “It’s just that we don’t know how to make them,” he said. {063-C06}

With such clues and mod­ern ge­net­ics, a re­vival has man­aged 300 threads to the square inch. {#threehundred} Varma called its air-conditioned weav­ing hut a mod­ern ju­gaad: the six­teen vil­lages had noth­ing of the kind.
~ But “three hun­dred to twelve hun­dred is a long way”, Varma said. Anyone buy­ing the new cloth must de­cide whether to com­pro­mise on the threads, or wait for the sci­ence to get there.

quote.text: That knowl­edge is lost in a gen­er­a­tion and they go on to do other things and the knowl­edge is com­pletely lost.

sections.label: Quest three
sections.head: Use it or lose it
sections.caption: why know-how needs practice
body: Fogbank, Ajay Shah said, was lost under very op­ti­mistic con­di­tions: mil­i­tary lev­els of bu­reau­cracy and record-keeping, and the orig­i­nal sci­en­tists still around. Stop doing some­thing for 30 or 40 years, and the tacit knowl­edge goes any­way. {063-C05}
Nuclear bombs, he ex­plained, do not keep the way a bul­let or an ar­tillery shell does. They con­tain elec­tri­cal parts and bat­ter­ies, and need a com­plex main­te­nance sched­ule.
## A Russian hy­poth­e­sis

That led Shah to a hy­poth­e­sis some peo­ple gen­uinely hold. The knowl­edge of that main­te­nance may have evap­o­rated when the Soviet Union col­lapsed, and “it is pos­si­ble that there is not a sin­gle work­ing nu­clear bomb in Russia today”. {#russia}
He called it a rea­son­able hy­poth­e­sis. The les­son, he said, is to store and log such knowl­edge; but if no­body is ac­tively doing some­thing, it will go away.
Amit Varma was re­minded of an army camp where a guard stood be­side a bench for decades be­cause no­body re­mem­bered the rea­son. {#reminded}

~ Shah won­dered whether the episode was made of sto­ries that ought to be movies. “These could all be movies, ac­tu­ally,” Varma said. “There’s so much human drama sur­round­ing each of these,” Shah replied.

quote.text: This kind of knowl­edge is pre­cious and we should do all we can to store it and log it.

sections.label: Quest four
sections.head: Mostly rubbish, sometimes gold
sections.caption: ancient texts and modern tests
body: Ancient texts, Ajay Shah said, are “cool and funny. They’re in­tended as hu­mour.” They hold the oc­ca­sional nugget of amaz­ing truth, and only test­ing finds it: some two thou­sand plants from tra­di­tional Chinese texts failed against malaria be­fore one worked. {#twothousand}
Yet Shah warned against the op­po­site error. “I think in the mod­ern world we are a lit­tle too ar­ro­gant in that we think we fab­ri­cate ev­ery­thing,” he said. {063-C08}

Citing James C Scott’s *Seeing Like a State*[[x9]], Shah said about half of the world’s 20 most im­por­tant drugs, in­clud­ing qui­nine, artemisinin and met­formin, began with plants and the knowl­edge of tra­di­tional peo­ple. {063-R14}
Modern sci­ence de­serves credit for re­fin­ing them, he added. Turning a flower into a pre­cise 500 mg slow-release pill is a great feat. {#metformin}
## Survivor bias

Amit Varma would treat tra­di­tion with deep scep­ti­cism, but never dis­miss it. {063-C09} Focusing only on the suc­cesses is sur­vivor bias[[x8]], he said: “the two thou­sand plants that did not pass the test are also im­por­tant.”
~ Old knowl­edge sys­tems, Varma added, built the­o­ries on first prin­ci­ples that came from a com­plete lack of what sci­ence knows today, so ex­tend­ing them gets you nowhere.

quote.text: Respect tra­di­tion but al­ways be scep­ti­cal.

portraits.caption: James C. Scott
portraits.credit: SOAS University of London, CC BY 3.0

sections.label: Quest five
sections.head: Flattened, then flourishing
sections.caption: Germany and Japan after the war
body: By 1945 Germany and Japan lay in ruins, Ajay Shah said: fac­to­ries de­stroyed, Tokyo’s wooden houses fire­bombed, and Germany’s in­sti­tu­tions first taken over by the Nazis, then wrecked in the war. It was, he said, “a bit of an iPhone and Wicked Witch cast­ing a spell idea”.
The knowl­edge in people’s heads was con­sid­er­able. In 1933, Shah noted, Germany had more Nobel lau­re­ates than the UK. {#nobel}
## Records and rights
West Germany had help that Urban’s naked hu­mans lack. Under the Marshall Plan money was avail­able, and books and man­u­als could be printed abroad and brought back. {#marshall}

Records were kept, so pre-war share­hold­ers were hon­oured. “So imag­ine there is a sec­ond world war, there’s com­plete dev­as­ta­tion, every fac­tory is gone, and Volkswagen comes back,” Shah said. {063-S11}

An old Weimar draft, with paci­fism added, be­came the new con­sti­tu­tion. Japan, after a suc­cess­ful pe­riod of American rule, got a paci­fist con­sti­tu­tion too. East Germany, under com­mu­nist rule, never quite re­cov­ered.

Amit Varma gave much of the credit to Ludwig Erhard, Adenauer’s fi­nance min­is­ter, who un­der­stood the value of free­dom and prop­erty rights. In that Germany, Varma said, “all the things we would dream of for India ac­tu­ally hap­pened.” {063-S12}
~ Both coun­tries, Shah said, de­ci­sively turned their backs on na­tion­al­ism and mil­i­tarism, and rein­vented them­selves.

quote.text: I would not have been able to pre­dict how well West Germany was going to take off
All your ma­te­rial goods are gone, but your knowl­edge is still in your head. And you can get ev­ery­thing back. All you need to do is build an iPhone six.

p3.title: Tales of the lost
p3.deck: Four stories of knowledge vanishing, and of the people hunting it down

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a scandalous fabric and its slow return
stories.head: Sixteen villages, one lost cloth
body: At the end of the 18th cen­tury, Amit Varma said, read­ing from the *Encyclopedia Americana*, women’s dress swapped stiff damasks, vel­vets, satins and silks for the cling­ing, short-waisted muslin gown. It caused a scan­dal in Britain.

A satire from around 1801 has a lady ask a milliner how to be dressed in the lat­est fash­ion. He has her re­move her bon­net, her tunic, her pet­ti­coat and her corset, and an­nounces: “In these days, if you want to be well dressed, you have to be well un­dressed.” {063-J05}
The finest of the fab­ric was Dhaka muslin[[x10]], from a plant on the banks of the Meghna in Bengal. Ordinary muslin has 20 to 40 threads per square inch. {#threads} Dhaka muslin had around 1,200.
Sixteen vil­lages made it, each doing one stage of the work. When the trade died, the know-how van­ished within a gen­er­a­tion, and the plant it­self could no longer be found. {063-S05}

The re­vival began with a 19th-century leaf. Researchers an­a­lysed its DNA, scanned the Meghna’s banks with satel­lite im­agery, and found a plant that shared 70 per cent of the original’s DNA. {#seventy}

Then they went to weavers across Bangladesh. Told the thread count, the weavers balked. One agreed. Housed in a tem­per­a­ture-controlled hut, he pro­duced a ver­sion with 300 threads. {#threehundred} Dresses made from it have sold for thou­sands of dol­lars.
~ Varma left Ajay Shah with a shop­ping dilemma for his next dress for Susan: com­pro­mise on the threads and still spend lots of money, or wait for the sci­ence to get there.
stories.why: Knowledge spread across many spe­cialised hands, with no­body writ­ing the process down, can van­ish within a gen­er­a­tion. Getting it back takes sur­viv­ing sam­ples, fin­ished cloth to re­verse-engineer and mod­ern sci­ence, and even then the re­cov­ery is par­tial. {063-C06}
stories.postscript: A friend of the hosts, Varma said, came up with “the big bong the­ory”: that ev­ery­thing re­ally started with big bongs. {063-J04}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Dhaka muslin’s lost threads

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the atomic recipe America could not follow
stories.head: The bomb that forgot its recipe
body: Aerogels are the light­est ma­te­ri­als known, Ajay Shah said: a litre might weigh two or three grams. {#aerogel} For one kind of American atomic bomb, built 40 or 50 years ago, a spe­cial aero­gel was de­vel­oped under the code name Fogbank.

During a main­te­nance over­haul some five or ten years ago, the United States found it had run out of Fogbank. Scientists went to the ar­chives, project re­ports and ex­per­i­ment logs, and could not make it.

So re­tired sci­en­tists were brought in and handed their own doc­u­ments. “You bloody now de­liver, you make Fogbank using your doc­u­ments,” Shah said. “These old hip­pies, they tried their magic, but no Fogbank.” {063-J10}
~ With au­di­tors scream­ing, about $70 mil­lion went into a brand new re­search project to reach the same aero­gel from scratch. {#seventymillion}
stories.why: Even with mil­i­tary lev­els of bu­reau­cracy and record-keeping, and with the orig­i­nal sci­en­tists still alive, know-how that had stopped being prac­tised for 30 or 40 years could not be re­cov­ered from doc­u­ments alone. {063-S06}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the Fogbank fiasco

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a Roman luxury and an Indian staple
stories.head: Hing, the poor man’s silphium
body: Silphium was the Romans’ prized herb, Ajay Shah said. They used its flow­ers, its stalk and its resinous gum, and could only for­age it from the wild. Within a cou­ple of hun­dred years, it was gone. {063-S04}
The Roman texts also name a backup for any­one too cheap or too poor to buy sil­phium resin: a cheap, harsh, pun­gent sub­sti­tute. “That backup plan was hing,” Shah said. {#hing}
Hing, or asafoetida, is a Ferula, and so is the plant a Turkish sci­en­tist has found in Greece and Turkey. “So this also con­nects,” Shah said.

~ Hing, he said, is “an ab­so­lute par­adise in Indian cook­ing”. If sil­phium re­turns, he imag­ines Roman recipes meet­ing Indian ones: per­haps a bet­ter curd rice made with fer­ula resin. He is wait­ing “with bated breath”.

quote.text: You feel the loss, you feel the hurt that there was some­thing beau­ti­ful that we knew and it was lost.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on silphium and hing

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on knowledge borrowed from goats and gorillas
stories.head: Follow the frisky goats
body: The story of cof­fee be­gins in Ethiopia, Ajay Shah said, with a shep­herd who no­ticed that his goats turned un­usu­ally frisky after eat­ing the plant’s berries. They would jump around and have a good time. {#goats}
So he tried chew­ing them him­self, and through hun­dreds of years of ran­dom ex­per­i­ments peo­ple got to roast­ing.
Scientists, Shah added, have seen some­thing sim­i­lar in the wild. “A go­rilla gets a stom­ach upset. The go­rilla walks 15 kilo­me­tres, finds one par­tic­u­lar plant, and eats it.” {063-S09}

~ Indigenous peo­ples, Shah said, gain ex­actly this kind of knowl­edge by watch­ing an­i­mals. The knowl­edge of the for­est is now “rapidly van­ish­ing”, and “we should do all we can to pro­tect that knowl­edge”.
stories.why: Much human knowl­edge was gath­ered by watch­ing na­ture rather than in­vented in lab­o­ra­to­ries. Coffee and medicines alike began this way, and the for­est peo­ples who hold such knowl­edge are los­ing it fast.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on goats, gorillas and coffee

quiz.q: How did Tu Youyou read the ancient Chinese text on wormwood differently from others?
quiz.a: As a cold ex­trac­tion: the plant soaked in water with­out heat­ing it.

quiz.q: Why, according to the 93-year-old founder, did a guard stand beside the bench?
quiz.a: The paint hadn’t dried yet; the camp had kept the guard for decades.

quiz.q: What cheap, harsh substitute for silphium resin do the Roman texts name?
quiz.a: Hing, or asafoetida, a Ferula plant prized in Indian cook­ing.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 63. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Tu Youyou (Bengt Nyman from Vaxholm, Sweden, CC BY 2.0); Friedrich Hayek (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0); James C. Scott (SOAS University of London, CC BY 3.0); Stefan Zweig (Franz Xaver Setzer (1886-1939), public domain); Isaac Asimov (Phillip Leonian [1] from New York World-Telegram & Sun.[2], public domain). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: The iPhone Thought Experiment
shelf.creator: Tim Urban
shelf.why: Shows how much of what we know de­pends on a ma­te­rial and so­cial web that no sin­gle per­son, or even all of hu­man­ity, could quickly re­build.

shelf.title: Tim Urban on The Lex Fridman Podcast
shelf.creator: Lex Fridman
shelf.why: Amit loved how Urban built up to it.

shelf.title: I, Pencil
shelf.creator: Leonard Read
shelf.why: A pen­cil nar­rates its own mak­ing from ma­te­ri­als and know-how scat­tered across many coun­tries, co­or­di­nated by prices with no one in charge.

shelf.title: The Use of Knowledge in Society
shelf.creator: Friedrich Hayek
shelf.why: Hayek’s ar­gu­ment that the knowl­edge needed to run an econ­omy is dis­persed among mil­lions of peo­ple, and that prices, not plan­ners, carry it: a lan­guage through which strangers tell each other what they want and lack.

shelf.title: Four Papers That Changed the World (Episode 41)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts ex­plain land­mark pa­pers in plain lan­guage, no­tably Coase on why firms exist and Hayek on how prices co­or­di­nate a so­ci­ety no plan­ner can grasp.

shelf.title: The Road
shelf.creator: Cormac McCarthy
shelf.why: A fa­ther and son walk through a post-apocalyptic land­scape: Ajay says it takes you deep in­side what it means to be a fa­ther and a son, and it is his image of the bar­barism that would fol­low if civilisation’s ma­te­rial base dis­ap­peared.

shelf.title: The Royal Game
shelf.creator: Stefan Zweig
shelf.why: Zweig’s mov­ing novella about a pris­oner in soli­tary con­fine­ment who plays chess against him­self until he can beat a world cham­pion.

shelf.title: This Be The Verse
shelf.creator: Philip Larkin
shelf.why: A great poem whose image of sed­i­ment deep­en­ing like a coastal shelf Amit uses for how knowl­edge builds up in lay­ers across gen­er­a­tions, and can be washed away.

shelf.title: This miracle plant was eaten into extinction 2,000 years ago -- or was it?
shelf.creator: Taras Grescoe
shelf.why: The full story of the lost Roman herb and the pos­si­ble mod­ern re­dis­cov­ery that Ajay is wait­ing for ‘with bated breath’.

shelf.title: The ancient fabric that no one knows how to make
shelf.creator: Zaria Gorvett
shelf.why: Amit says Gorvett has writ­ten many other ex­cel­lent pieces on sim­i­lar sub­jects that are worth check­ing out.

shelf.title: Fogbank (Wikipedia)
shelf.why: Background on the clas­si­fied US nu­clear aero­gel whose recipe was lost and had to be rein­vented at great cost.

shelf.title: From bark to weed: The history of artemisinin
shelf.creator: Claude Faurant
shelf.why: The his­tory be­hind how an an­cient Chinese rem­edy be­came the main mod­ern treat­ment for malaria.

shelf.title: Tu Youyou on the Nobel Prize website
shelf.why: A pro­file of the non-PhD re­searcher whose close read­ing of clas­si­cal Chinese pro­duced artemisinin.

shelf.title: Seeing Like a State
shelf.creator: James C Scott
shelf.why: Scott’s ac­count of how state schemes to im­prove the human con­di­tion fail when bu­reau­cra­cies can­not ‘see’ the so­ci­ety they rule, with a tool­kit (state leg­i­bil­ity, high mod­ernism, metis) you can apply al­most any­where.

shelf.title: Beware of Quacks. Alternative Medicine is Injurious to Health
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s own piece on why tra­di­tional and al­ter­na­tive medicine de­serve deep skep­ti­cism.

shelf.title: Bad Science
shelf.creator: Ben Goldacre
shelf.why: A great book on see­ing through med­i­cal claims with sci­en­tific ev­i­dence.

shelf.title: Trick or Treatment?
shelf.creator: Simon Singh and Edzard Erst
shelf.why: A sci­ence-based look at al­ter­na­tive medicine, which fits Amit’s line: re­spect tra­di­tion, but al­ways be skep­ti­cal.

shelf.title: Abby Philips Fights for Science and Medicine (Episode 310 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A long de­fence of sci­en­tific medicine from liver doc­tor Abby Philips, on the ten­sion be­tween doing right by pa­tients and giv­ing them what they want.

shelf.title: Postwar
shelf.creator: Tony Judt
shelf.why: Amit calls it a mas­ter­piece on post-war Europe and its re­cov­ery.

shelf.title: On the Natural History of Destruction
shelf.creator: WG Sebald
shelf.why: A mas­ter­piece with many pages on Dresden.

shelf.title: Orienting
shelf.creator: Pallavi Aiyar
shelf.why: A trav­el­ogue that reads like a beau­ti­ful essay, by a ‘spec­tac­u­larly good writer’.

shelf.title: Pallavi Aiyar Has Seen the World (Episode 351 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A long con­ver­sa­tion with the au­thor of Orienting.

shelf.title: Nightfall
shelf.creator: Isaac Asimov
shelf.why: He says noth­ing more be­cause any­thing more would be a spoiler.

laughs.text: On the witch leav­ing 7.3 bil­lion naked peo­ple: Amit says ‘you could argue that there are any­way, they’re just putting some clothes on,’ then cites Bob Dylan that ‘even the pres­i­dent of the United States must stand naked.’
Amit on maybe writ­ing a book about re­boot­ing civil­i­sa­tion: ‘after the other fif­teen I have planned.’
Amit, a Bengali, on Bengal’s con­tri­bu­tions: a friend came up with ‘the big bong the­ory, that ev­ery­thing re­ally started with big bongs, as it were.’

A satire from around 1801 on see-through muslin: a milliner gets a lady to re­move her bon­net, tunic, pet­ti­coat and corset, then an­nounces, ‘In these days, if you want to be well dressed, you have to be well un­dressed.’ Amit calls it a very male-gaze joke about a very male-gaze so­ci­ety.

Amit quotes Hippocrates’ sil­phium treat­ment for a pro­lapse (‘When the gut pro­trudes and will not re­main in its place... apply as a cataplasm’), then adds: ‘So you can see why this is of spe­cial in­ter­est to me.’
Amit on Calcutta’s re­tail scene look­ing like 1979: a coin-operated weigh­ing ma­chine from 1964 where ‘my weight went down each time be­cause I was los­ing a one rupee coin.’
Amit on being a probashi, a Bengali who doesn’t live in Bengal: ‘A cuss word. I mean, there are peo­ple who are proud Probashis, but what­ever.’

Ajay on re­tired Fogbank sci­en­tists being handed their own doc­u­ments: ‘You bloody now de­liver, you make Fogbank using your doc­u­ments.’ Then ‘these, you know, old hip­pies, they tried their magic, but no Fogbank.’
Ajay on an­cient texts: ‘Ancient texts are cool and funny. They’re in­tended as humor.’ He later says the same of a newly found Aramaic text.
Frédéric Bastiat’s essay on how the city of Paris gets fed with no one plan­ning it, cited next to I, Pencil as an ex­am­ple of de­cen­tralised co­or­di­na­tion.
Pliny the Elder’s Natural History, which records that only one stalk of sil­phium was found and it was given to Emperor Nero.
Petronius in the Satyricon, mock­ing see-through muslin by say­ing a bride might as well stand naked, which shows the moral panic over the fab­ric goes back to an­cient times.
Alfred Russel Wallace: on how gru­elling malaria is, Ajay says ‘most of us are not lucky enough to be Alfred Russel Wallace and carry some­thing cool out of that jour­ney.’
Ignaz Semmelweis, re­called from an ear­lier episode: ten per­cent of peo­ple who en­tered ma­ter­nity wards died, which helps ex­plain the ap­peal of harm­less sugar-pill home­opa­thy.
